- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. 18	                                           Abstract: This study was conducted to determine if the acute: chronic workload ratio (ACWR) is
19	                                           related to the incidence of non-contact injuries. The purpose is to compare the external load of injured
20	                                           and non-injured soccer players with the same characteristics, such as position and age. The present
21	                                           analysis considers both the four and the two weeks preceding an injury. Physical characteristics
22	                                           were recorded and analyzed through global positioning systems (GPS) evaluation over one season of
23	                                           24 competitive microcycles, 144 training sessions, and 32 matches in a total of 35 professional soccer
24	                                           players from the Greek Super League 1 and Super League 2. The loads calculated were total distance
25	                                           (TD), 15–20 km/h, 20–25 km/h, 25–30 km/h, accelerations (ACC) > 2.5 m/s2 , and decelerations
26	                                           (DEC) > 2.5 m/s2 ). Nine injured athletes exceeded the critical threshold of an ACWR > 1.3 several
27	                                           times compared with non-injured athletes that did not reach this level. The present study showed
28	                                           that ACWR is related to a subsequent occurrence of injury but that the threshold of an ACWR can
29	                                           vary. This seems to be mainly influenced by assessing the load of the last two weeks compared with

73	                                 Research on this specific subject has increased in recent years [13]. The most recent
74	                           research has recorded the characteristics of the external burden and quantified them through
75	                           the ACWR method to predict the probability of a non-contact injury in percentage terms.
76	                           More specifically, some studies, such as Bowen et al. [14], fully support the results of
77	                           the relationship between ACWR and non-contact injuries in soccer and rugby which
78	                           correlate to a significantly lower burden over the last week compared with that over
79	                           the previous three weeks [15] or the continued high burden of the high risk of injury
80	                           through ACWR [10–12,16–18]. In contrast, other studies report that the reduced chronic
81	                           load compared with the immediate (last week) load can cause injury to an athlete [19,20].
82	                                 On the other hand, further research does not support the relationship of ACWR with
83	                           non-contact injuries. More specifically, no differences were found in accumulated weekly
84	                           loads and ACWR calculations regarding injured athletes [21], a conclusion which was
85	                           supported by related research [22–24], while Impellizzeri et al. [13] mentions that ACWR
86	                           is a rescaling of the explanatory variable (AL, numerator), in turn magnifying its effect
87	                           estimates and decreasing its variance despite conferring no predictive advantage.
88	                                 No soccer research to date has investigated external load in two different periods (the
89	                           fourth and second week before injury), only the internal load of the session rating of the
90	                           perceived exertion (s-RPE). Delecroix et al. [20], reporting on acute: chronic workloads
91	                           using combinations of two, three, and four weeks, provided some evidence to predict an
92	                           injury, but not to an absolute degree. Fanchini et al. [22] provided evidence for internal
93	                           load as a risk factor for non-contact injury.
94	                                 Our study will hence make a distinct contribution to the data comparing the burden
95	                           in injured and uninjured soccer players, with evidence that will concern the separate
96	                           management that should exist in the four weeks and the two weeks before the injury. The
97	                           principal aim is to ensure the health of soccer players, freeing clubs to a large extent from
98	                           the additional financial exposure and rating losses that follow soccer injuries [25].

100	                           2. Materials and Methods
101	                           2.1. Participants
102	                                 Thirty-five Greek professional soccer players (21.1 ± 0.6 years, 180.4 ± 2.6 cm,
103	                           76.2 ± 3.8 kg, 6.5 ± 1.1% body fat) participated in this study. Before the start of the study,
104	                           all testing procedures were fully explained in detail to participants. A consent form for
105	                           participation in the study was read and then signed by the participants. Moreover, the
106	                           study was approved by the ethical committee of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki
107	                           (96/2021) in accordance with the ethical standards in sport and exercise research.
108	
109	                           2.2. Experimental Design
110	                                The external load of soccer players was recorded and evaluated using GPS technology
111	                           (Vector S7, Catapult, Catapult Sports Ltd., Melbourne, Victoria, Australia) at a frequency of
112	                           10 Hz, the reliability of which was demonstrated in research by Clavel et al. [26] during
113	                           the entire 2021–2022 season. In total, the study lasted for 24 competitive microcycles and
114	                           144 training units. During the specific weeks studied, there were 16 microcycles, during
115	                           which there was an official match in the middle of the week. Both the 32 official matches
116	                           and the training sessions were held on outdoor pitches with natural grass.
117	
118	                           2.3. External Load Analysis
119	                                Subjects wore a GPS device during all training sessions and official matches, which
120	                           was placed on their upper back (the GPS device is worn in a specially designed vest).
121	                           Each player used the same device during the research period. High-speed running of
122	                           14.4–19.8 km/h, very high-speed running of 19.8–25.0 km/h, and sprints of >25.0 km/h
123	                           were evaluated, as well as accelerations with deceleration in zones of <2.5 m/s2 .
124	                                Loads were analyzed into weekly plans, where training days were separated. The days
125	                           with a minus (MD-) refer to the days that are before the next match and the days with a plus
126	                           (MD+) refer to the days after the previous match. Each weekly block consists of the weekly

128	
129

132	                           match day (MD) and all training days are coded as MD-6, MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2,
133	                           MD-1. For nine-day microcycles, match—MD + 1 = recovery, MD + 2 = rest, MD-7, MD-6,
134	                           MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1; for eight-day microcycles, match—MD + 1 = recovery,
135	                           MD + 2 = rest, MD-6, MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1; for seven-day microcycles, match
136	                           − MD + 1 = recovery, MD + 2 = rest, MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1; and finally, for
137	                           six-day microcycles, MD + 1 match = recovery, MD + 2 = rest, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1.
138	                           For the reliability and validity of the study, only data from soccer players performing the
139	                           full daily training program and participating in matches accordingly were used, and data
140	                           from goalkeepers and the soccer players whose total load (TL) was manipulated during
141	                           this period due to fatigue or injury management were removed. All athletes were fully
142	                           familiarized with the experimental procedures. Soccer players who had completed at least
143	                           90% of the total obligations (training, matches) during one week participated in the research
144	                           process. ACWR used the data collected at four weeks and two weeks to create the first
145	                           value before the microcycle in which the soccer player was injured. Chronic workload was
146	                           calculated as the four-week and two-week immediate workload, and ACWR was calculated
147	                           by dividing the immediate by the chronic workload (load accumulated during the week
148	                           the athlete was injured/average of the previous four weeks or two weeks). Risk zones were
149	                           defined as values <0.80 and >1.3 [10].
150	
151	                           2.4. Definition of Injury
152	                                 Only non-contact injuries were included in the study. A doctor always gave the final
153	                           opinion on an injury after the necessary tests had been conducted. Injuries were classified
154	                           as minimal (1–3 days lost of active participation), mild (4–7 days lost), moderate (1–4 weeks
155	                           lost), and severe (4+ weeks lost) [27]. In total, the injuries recorded in the survey were mild
156	                           and moderate, according to the previous formulation.
157	                                 Injury incidence was reported in absolute numbers and as an injury incidence rate for
158	                           the number of injuries per 1000 h of participation in matches and training [27].
159	
160	                           2.5. Statistical Analysis
161	                                IBM SPSS, version 25 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) software was used for statistical
162	                           analysis. Continuous variables were expressed as mean with standard deviation. Because
163	                           of the small sample size (N = 18), we used nonparametric controls. For all tests, statistical
164	                           differences were determined to be significant at p < 0.05.
165	                                We used the Wilcoxon test to compare the differences between the two comparison
166	                           groups (injured athletes vs. non-injured athletes). Each observation in one sample is linked
167	                           to an observation in the other sample as well (same group, same position, and similar age).
168	
169	                           3. Results
170	                                Nine soccer players were injured without contact during competitive microcycles.
171	                           Of these, four were injured in the hip adductors, two were injured in the area of their
172	                           biceps femoris, another two experienced a muscle injury in the gastrocnemius, while one
173	                           was injured in the quadriceps muscle. The overall rate of non-contact injuries during the
174	                           competition season (over 24 microcycles) was 4.5/1000 h.

529	                           directly associated with injury risk (except distance at high speed). These results contrast

531	                           at high rates during training to protect against subsequent soft tissue injury. Moreover,
532	                           according to Buchheit [29], and since soccer players have international obligations with
533	                           their national teams, contradictory data exist due to the different recording systems used
534	                           by the teams for which they play, which necessarily makes predicting non-contact injuries
535	                           much more difficult.
536	                                Our study found a correlation between ACWR scores and injury frequency over an
537	                           entire season in professional soccer players. In the current study, nine injured soccer players
538	                           repeatedly received a more significant load than the previous four (ACWR4), especially
539	                           at two weeks (ACWR2). Essentially, it is observed that the considerably increased load in
540	                           one microcycle, always compared with the previous four and two weeks, does not keep a
541	                           soccer player in a good playing condition which will protect them against injury during
542	                           the game to be played at the end of that particular microcycle.
543	                                In addition, the current research results show that when the volume of running speed
544	                           with higher intensities (15–20 km/h, 20–25 km/h, <25 km/h) increased, non-contact injuries
545	                           occurred. A possible relationship between accelerations and decelerations in the occurrence
546	                           of non-contact injury was also observed, as confirmed by Schache et al. [30], who report
547	                           that these concentric and eccentric movements are responsible for most specific injuries.
548	                           Essentially, we have to focus on high-speed running (15–20 km/h, 20–25 km/h, <25 km/h)
549	                           which, according to our research, has a greater negative impact on a football player when
550	                           they exceed the previous load. This was found mainly in the analysis of two, and less
551	                           so in four, weeks. Limitations of this study could include that the football players who
552	                           participated in the research may not have had exactly the same participation time in the
553	                           team’s official match.
554	
555	                           5. Conclusions
556	                                  In the present study, both models comparing ACWR4 and ACWR2 give indications
557	                           of the possible occurrence of non-contact injury in professional soccer players. It was
558	                           observed that the ACWR2 model may be a more sensitive indicator as the differences were
559	                           more pronounced in more of the examined variables. From the above, it can be seen that
560	                           staff dealing with the physical condition and prevention of injuries in professional soccer
561	                           players should consider the indications from the ACWR4 and ACWR2 indicators. We
562	                           suggest the ACWR2 model as the most applicable as it is more immediate (two weeks
563	                           versus four weeks) and thus a soccer scientist will be able to control the loads better since he
564	                           will need fewer days to analyze the data (of training and matches). Moreover, because the
565	                           burden on soccer players not only consists of running but can also include strength training,
566	                           it is recommended that future research include these elements of burden in attempts to
567	                           predict injury.

Useful to Prevent Injuries in Soccer?
Andreas Fousekis 1 , Konstantinos Fousekis 2 , Georgios Fousekis 3 , Nikolaos Vaitsis 4 , Ioannis Terzidis 1 ,
Kosmas Christoulas 1 , Yiannis Michailidis 1, * , Athanasios Mandroukas 1 and Thomas Metaxas 1

                                           *   Correspondence: ioannimd@phed.auth.gr; Tel.: +30-231-099-2233


                                           Abstract: This study was conducted to determine if the acute: chronic workload ratio (ACWR) is
                                           related to the incidence of non-contact injuries. The purpose is to compare the external load of injured
                                           and non-injured soccer players with the same characteristics, such as position and age. The present
                                           analysis considers both the four and the two weeks preceding an injury. Physical characteristics
                                           were recorded and analyzed through global positioning systems (GPS) evaluation over one season of
                                           24 competitive microcycles, 144 training sessions, and 32 matches in a total of 35 professional soccer
                                           players from the Greek Super League 1 and Super League 2. The loads calculated were total distance
                                           (TD), 15–20 km/h, 20–25 km/h, 25–30 km/h, accelerations (ACC) > 2.5 m/s2 , and decelerations
                                           (DEC) > 2.5 m/s2 ). Nine injured athletes exceeded the critical threshold of an ACWR > 1.3 several
                                           times compared with non-injured athletes that did not reach this level. The present study showed
                                           that ACWR is related to a subsequent occurrence of injury but that the threshold of an ACWR can
                                           vary. This seems to be mainly influenced by assessing the load of the last two weeks compared with

Appl. Sci. 2023, 13, 495. https://doi.org/10.3390/app13010495                                                  https://www.mdpi.com/journal/applsci
 Appl. Sci. 2023, 13, 495                                                                                            2 of 8




                                 Research on this specific subject has increased in recent years [13]. The most recent
                           research has recorded the characteristics of the external burden and quantified them through
                           the ACWR method to predict the probability of a non-contact injury in percentage terms.
                           More specifically, some studies, such as Bowen et al. [14], fully support the results of
                           the relationship between ACWR and non-contact injuries in soccer and rugby which
                           correlate to a significantly lower burden over the last week compared with that over
                           the previous three weeks [15] or the continued high burden of the high risk of injury
                           through ACWR [10–12,16–18]. In contrast, other studies report that the reduced chronic
                           load compared with the immediate (last week) load can cause injury to an athlete [19,20].
                                 On the other hand, further research does not support the relationship of ACWR with
                           non-contact injuries. More specifically, no differences were found in accumulated weekly
                           loads and ACWR calculations regarding injured athletes [21], a conclusion which was
                           supported by related research [22–24], while Impellizzeri et al. [13] mentions that ACWR
                           is a rescaling of the explanatory variable (AL, numerator), in turn magnifying its effect
                           estimates and decreasing its variance despite conferring no predictive advantage.
                                 No soccer research to date has investigated external load in two different periods (the
                           fourth and second week before injury), only the internal load of the session rating of the
                           perceived exertion (s-RPE). Delecroix et al. [20], reporting on acute: chronic workloads
                           using combinations of two, three, and four weeks, provided some evidence to predict an
                           injury, but not to an absolute degree. Fanchini et al. [22] provided evidence for internal
                           load as a risk factor for non-contact injury.
                                 Our study will hence make a distinct contribution to the data comparing the burden
                           in injured and uninjured soccer players, with evidence that will concern the separate
                           management that should exist in the four weeks and the two weeks before the injury. The
                           principal aim is to ensure the health of soccer players, freeing clubs to a large extent from
                           the additional financial exposure and rating losses that follow soccer injuries [25].

                           2. Materials and Methods
                           2.1. Participants
                                 Thirty-five Greek professional soccer players (21.1 ± 0.6 years, 180.4 ± 2.6 cm,
                           76.2 ± 3.8 kg, 6.5 ± 1.1% body fat) participated in this study. Before the start of the study,
                           all testing procedures were fully explained in detail to participants. A consent form for
                           participation in the study was read and then signed by the participants. Moreover, the
                           study was approved by the ethical committee of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki
                           (96/2021) in accordance with the ethical standards in sport and exercise research.

                           2.2. Experimental Design
                                The external load of soccer players was recorded and evaluated using GPS technology
                           (Vector S7, Catapult, Catapult Sports Ltd., Melbourne, Victoria, Australia) at a frequency of
                           10 Hz, the reliability of which was demonstrated in research by Clavel et al. [26] during
                           the entire 2021–2022 season. In total, the study lasted for 24 competitive microcycles and
                           144 training units. During the specific weeks studied, there were 16 microcycles, during
                           which there was an official match in the middle of the week. Both the 32 official matches
                           and the training sessions were held on outdoor pitches with natural grass.

                           2.3. External Load Analysis
                                Subjects wore a GPS device during all training sessions and official matches, which
                           was placed on their upper back (the GPS device is worn in a specially designed vest).
                           Each player used the same device during the research period. High-speed running of
                           14.4–19.8 km/h, very high-speed running of 19.8–25.0 km/h, and sprints of >25.0 km/h
                           were evaluated, as well as accelerations with deceleration in zones of <2.5 m/s2 .
                                Loads were analyzed into weekly plans, where training days were separated. The days
                           with a minus (MD-) refer to the days that are before the next match and the days with a plus
                           (MD+) refer to the days after the previous match. Each weekly block consists of the weekly
 Appl. Sci. 2023, 13, 495                                                                                             3 of 8




                           match day (MD) and all training days are coded as MD-6, MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2,
                           MD-1. For nine-day microcycles, match—MD + 1 = recovery, MD + 2 = rest, MD-7, MD-6,
                           MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1; for eight-day microcycles, match—MD + 1 = recovery,
                           MD + 2 = rest, MD-6, MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1; for seven-day microcycles, match
                           − MD + 1 = recovery, MD + 2 = rest, MD-5, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1; and finally, for
                           six-day microcycles, MD + 1 match = recovery, MD + 2 = rest, MD-4, MD-3, MD-2, MD-1.
                           For the reliability and validity of the study, only data from soccer players performing the
                           full daily training program and participating in matches accordingly were used, and data
                           from goalkeepers and the soccer players whose total load (TL) was manipulated during
                           this period due to fatigue or injury management were removed. All athletes were fully
                           familiarized with the experimental procedures. Soccer players who had completed at least
                           90% of the total obligations (training, matches) during one week participated in the research
                           process. ACWR used the data collected at four weeks and two weeks to create the first
                           value before the microcycle in which the soccer player was injured. Chronic workload was
                           calculated as the four-week and two-week immediate workload, and ACWR was calculated
                           by dividing the immediate by the chronic workload (load accumulated during the week
                           the athlete was injured/average of the previous four weeks or two weeks). Risk zones were
                           defined as values <0.80 and >1.3 [10].

                           2.4. Definition of Injury
                                 Only non-contact injuries were included in the study. A doctor always gave the final
                           opinion on an injury after the necessary tests had been conducted. Injuries were classified
                           as minimal (1–3 days lost of active participation), mild (4–7 days lost), moderate (1–4 weeks
                           lost), and severe (4+ weeks lost) [27]. In total, the injuries recorded in the survey were mild
                           and moderate, according to the previous formulation.
                                 Injury incidence was reported in absolute numbers and as an injury incidence rate for
                           the number of injuries per 1000 h of participation in matches and training [27].

                           2.5. Statistical Analysis
                                IBM SPSS, version 25 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) software was used for statistical
                           analysis. Continuous variables were expressed as mean with standard deviation. Because
                           of the small sample size (N = 18), we used nonparametric controls. For all tests, statistical
                           differences were determined to be significant at p < 0.05.
                                We used the Wilcoxon test to compare the differences between the two comparison
                           groups (injured athletes vs. non-injured athletes). Each observation in one sample is linked
                           to an observation in the other sample as well (same group, same position, and similar age).

                           3. Results
                                Nine soccer players were injured without contact during competitive microcycles.
                           Of these, four were injured in the hip adductors, two were injured in the area of their
                           biceps femoris, another two experienced a muscle injury in the gastrocnemius, while one
                           was injured in the quadriceps muscle. The overall rate of non-contact injuries during the
                           competition season (over 24 microcycles) was 4.5/1000 h.

                           3.1. ACWR at Four Weeks before Injury

                                        Using ACWR for injury risk and comparing external loads, it was found that the ratio
                                  of immediate to chronic loads (absolute total distance) predicted injuries in elite rugby
                                  players [12]. Bowen et al. [11], investigating data from young elite-level soccer players,

                           showed that three-week accelerations in particular were the strongest predictor of injury.
                           Decelerations were particularly associated with a greater risk of non-contact injury by the
                           same authors in 2019, and, in collaboration with professional soccer players, ACWR was
                           directly associated with injury risk (except distance at high speed). These results contrast
                           with Malone et al. [28], who concluded that athletes should perform maximal velocities
                           at high rates during training to protect against subsequent soft tissue injury. Moreover,
                           according to Buchheit [29], and since soccer players have international obligations with
                           their national teams, contradictory data exist due to the different recording systems used
                           by the teams for which they play, which necessarily makes predicting non-contact injuries
                           much more difficult.
                                Our study found a correlation between ACWR scores and injury frequency over an
                           entire season in professional soccer players. In the current study, nine injured soccer players
                           repeatedly received a more significant load than the previous four (ACWR4), especially
                           at two weeks (ACWR2). Essentially, it is observed that the considerably increased load in
                           one microcycle, always compared with the previous four and two weeks, does not keep a
                           soccer player in a good playing condition which will protect them against injury during
                           the game to be played at the end of that particular microcycle.
                                In addition, the current research results show that when the volume of running speed
                           with higher intensities (15–20 km/h, 20–25 km/h, <25 km/h) increased, non-contact injuries
                           occurred. A possible relationship between accelerations and decelerations in the occurrence
                           of non-contact injury was also observed, as confirmed by Schache et al. [30], who report
                           that these concentric and eccentric movements are responsible for most specific injuries.
                           Essentially, we have to focus on high-speed running (15–20 km/h, 20–25 km/h, <25 km/h)
                           which, according to our research, has a greater negative impact on a football player when
                           they exceed the previous load. This was found mainly in the analysis of two, and less
                           so in four, weeks. Limitations of this study could include that the football players who
                           participated in the research may not have had exactly the same participation time in the
                           team’s official match.

                           5. Conclusions
                                  In the present study, both models comparing ACWR4 and ACWR2 give indications
                           of the possible occurrence of non-contact injury in professional soccer players. It was
                           observed that the ACWR2 model may be a more sensitive indicator as the differences were
                           more pronounced in more of the examined variables. From the above, it can be seen that
                           staff dealing with the physical condition and prevention of injuries in professional soccer
                           players should consider the indications from the ACWR4 and ACWR2 indicators. We
                           suggest the ACWR2 model as the most applicable as it is more immediate (two weeks
                           versus four weeks) and thus a soccer scientist will be able to control the loads better since he
                           will need fewer days to analyze the data (of training and matches). Moreover, because the
                           burden on soccer players not only consists of running but can also include strength training,
                           it is recommended that future research include these elements of burden in attempts to
                           predict injury.

11	 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
12	 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
13	 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
14	 "sports": ["Soccer"],
15	 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
16	 "evidenceSummary": "Observational GPS study of 80 professional outfield players from one La Liga club over four seasons, comparing starters (more than 60 minutes played in the previous match) with non-starters across 6-day (3 training sessions) and 7-day (4 sessions) microcycles, under two post-match plans: compensatory training on MD+1 (P1) or MD+2 (P2). Non-starters accumulated more training load than starters in most variables, with the largest differences under P1; under P2, starters had higher load, monotony and strain. The exception was locomotor load in the 7-day week.",
17	 "screeningLimitations": "Observational design from one club, with no competition load, internal response, or wellness data, so results may not generalise. The group sizes (starter n=1607, non-starter n=3104) are reported without defining the unit, so the number of independent players is unclear.",
18	 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the study as showing that non-starters should always get more load, when it only describes how one club distributed training across its weekly plans.",
19	 "paper": {
20	   "year": 2024,
21	   "citation": "Marín K, Castellano J. Two periodization strategies in professional football and their influence on accumulated training load and its distribution: Differences between starters and non-starters. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.",
22	   "doi": "10.1080/02640414.2024.2318061",
23	   "abstract": "Compared weekly training load, training monotony and training strain in 80 professional football players, using GPS. Two microcycle lengths (6 and 7 days between matches) and two post-match periodization strategies (compensatory session on MD+1 or MD+2) were analysed separately for starters and non-starters.",
24	   "tldr": "Non-starters carried more training load than starters in most weekly measures, and the timing of the post-match session changed how load was shared. Plan load separately by playing status, session timing and microcycle length.",
25	   "methods": "Four seasons of GPS data (10 Hz) from training sessions only; match-day data were excluded. Variables were total distance, Player Load, high-speed and sprint distance, accelerations and decelerations, with monotony and strain derived from them. Groups were compared with Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests with Cohen's d effect sizes.",
26	   "findings": "Non-starters accumulated higher load than starters in most variables in both microcycle lengths, with moderate to large effects under P1 in high-speed running, Player Load and total distance. Under P2, starters had higher load, monotony and strain than under P1. The 7-day week was associated with higher load for both groups, and locomotor load in that week was the exception to the non-starter pattern.",
27	   "limitations": "Observational design from a single club. Competition load was excluded by design, and heart rate, perceived exertion and wellness data were not included. The paper notes that congested schedules and travel were not modelled.",
28	   "practicalImplications": "Set the compensatory session by playing status. Where it cannot fall on match day, train non-starters on MD+1 to keep the stimulus close to competition. Use MD+2 to give starters more load when they can take it. Check monotony and strain when moving between 3- and 4-session weeks.",
29	   "athleteDev": "Use the load comparison to set compensatory sessions for non-starters and recovery sessions for starters, and check monotony and strain when microcycle length changes.",

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                            ARTICLE HISTORY
    This study compared weekly training-load (TL), training-monotony (TM), and training-strain (TS) in 80                               Received 20 August 2023
    professional football players (28.1 ± 3.2 yrs, 78.0 ± 5.9 kg, and 182.0 ± 4.8 cm), considering two lengths (6                       Accepted 5 February 2024
    and 7 days between matches), two types of periodization strategies (placing the compensatory session in                             KEYWORDS
    MD+1 [P1] or MD+2 [P2] post-match-day) and two players’ status, starters, and non-starters. Using Global                            Football; team sport;
    Positioning Technology, the monitored variables were: Player Load (PL), Total Distance (TD), distances at                           monitoring; training
    various speeds (>21 [HSR], >24 [VHSR], and > 27 [SPR] km·h−1), number of accelerations (>2 m·s−2, ACC),                             demand; GPS
    and decelerations (<-2 m·s−2, DEC). Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney non-parametric statistical tests
    were used for loading strategy differences. In both lengths and periodization strategies of the micro-
    cycles, non-starters trained more than starters. There were differences in the quantity (TL) and distribu­
    tion (TM and TS) demand considering the micro-cycle’s length and periodization strategy. In
    MD+1 (P1), non-starters accumulated higher TL, showing moderate to large Cohen’s d magnitudes in
    HSR, VHSR, SPR, PL, and TD. For starters, training in MD+2 (P2) resulted in higher values (p < 0.05) of TL, TM
    and TS. The coaching staff needs to anticipate TL, TM, and TS by considering players’ status, periodization
    strategy, and the number of training sessions between matches.

                                                                                                                                                                                                               ABSTRACT
                                                                                                                                                 BJKRNSEN, T., M. WERNBOM, A. KIRKETEIG, G. PAULSEN, L. SAMNKY, L. B%KKEN, D. CAMERON-SMITH, S.
                                                                                                                                                 BERNTSEN, and T. RAASTAD. Type 1 Muscle Fiber Hypertrophy after Blood Flow–restricted Training in Powerlifters. Med. Sci.
                                                                                                                                                 Sports Exerc., Vol. 51, No. 2, pp. 288–298, 2019. Purpose: To investigate the effects of blood flow–restricted resistance exercise
                                                                                                                                                 (BFRRE) on myofiber areas (MFA), number of myonuclei and satellite cells (SC), muscle size and strength in powerlifters. Methods: Seventeen
                                                                                                                                                 national level powerlifters (25 T 6 yr [mean T SD], 15 men) were randomly assigned to either a BFRRE group (n = 9) performing two
                                                                                                                                                 blocks (weeks 1 and 3) of five BFRRE front squat sessions within a 6.5-wk training period, or a conventional training group (Con; n = 8)
                                                                                                                                                 performing front squats at 60%–85% of one-repetition maximum (1RM). The BFRRE consisted of four sets (first and last set to voluntary
                                                                                                                                                 failure) at ~30% of 1RM. Muscle biopsies were obtained from m. vastus lateralis (VL) and analyzed for MFA, myonuclei, SC and
                                                                                                                                                 capillaries. Cross-sectional areas (CSA) of VL and m. rectus femoris were measured by ultrasonography. Strength was evaluated by
                                                                                                                                                 maximal voluntary isokinetic torque (MVIT) in knee extension and 1RM in front squat. Results: BFRRE induced selective increases in
                                                                                                                                                 type I MFA (BFRRE: 12% vs Con: 0%, P G 0.01) and myonuclear number (BFRRE: 18% vs Con: 0%, P = 0.02). Type II MFA was
                                                                                                                                                 unaltered in both groups. BFRRE induced greater changes in VL CSA (7.7% vs 0.5%, P = 0.04), which correlated with the increases in
                                                                                                                                                 MFA of type I fibers (r = 0.81, P = 0.02). No group differences were observed in SC and strength changes, although MVIT increased
                                                                                                                                                 with BFRRE (P = 0.04), whereas 1RM increased in Con (P = 0.02). Conclusions: Two blocks of low-load BFRRE in the front
                                                                                                                                                 squat exercise resulted in increased quadriceps CSA associated with preferential hypertrophy and myonuclear addition in type 1 fibers
                                                                                                                                                 of national level powerlifters. Key Words: ISCHEMIC TRAINING; KAATSU; MYOGENIC STEM CELLS, MYONUCLEAR
                                                                                                                                                 ADDITION, MYONUCLEAR DOMAIN, ATHLETES

 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised controlled trial of 17 national-level powerlifters (15 men, 2 women), allocated to a blood flow-restricted low-load front squat group (BFRRE, n=9) or a conventional heavy front squat group (n=8) within a 6.5-week strength programme. The BFRRE group showed larger increases in type I muscle fibre area (12% vs 0%) and type I myonuclei (18% vs 0%), and larger vastus lateralis cross-sectional area (7.7% vs 0.5%, P=0.04). Knee extension torque rose in the BFRRE group only and front squat 1RM rose in the control group only, with no between-group difference in strength.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Small groups (9 and 8) and a short intervention; the authors note that statistical power may have been too low for smaller effects in type II fibres. Cuff pressure was set with elastic wraps rather than tightly controlled, the strength test used the front squat, which several lifters were not well familiarised with, and the control group completed more high-load front squat sessions (16 vs 6).",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the fibre and size results as evidence that blood flow restriction improves maximal strength, when the trial found no between-group difference in strength.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Bjørnsen T, Wernbom M, Kirketeig A, Paulsen G, Samnøy L, Bækken L, et al. Type 1 Muscle Fiber Hypertrophy after Blood Flow-restricted Training in Powerlifters. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(2):288-298.",
   "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000001775",
   "abstract": "Seventeen national-level powerlifters were randomised to two 1-week blocks of low-load blood flow-restricted front squats or conventional heavy front squat training within a 6.5-week programme. Muscle biopsies, ultrasound measures and strength tests were taken before and after the programme.",
   "tldr": "Two short blocks of low-load blood flow-restricted squats added to a strength programme produced more type I fibre growth and quadriceps size than heavy squats in elite powerlifters, but not more maximal strength. For strength-focused athletes this is a muscle-size finding only.",
   "methods": "Randomised controlled trial in 17 national-level powerlifters. The BFRRE group performed four front squat sets at about 30% of 1RM with thigh pressure of about 120 mm Hg in weeks 1 and 3; the control group performed heavy front squats at 60-85% of 1RM. Outcomes were muscle fibre area, myonuclei, satellite cells, ultrasound muscle size, isokinetic knee extension torque and front squat 1RM.",
   "findings": "The BFRRE group had larger increases in type I fibre area (12% vs 0%) and type I myonuclei (18% vs 0%), and larger vastus lateralis cross-sectional area (7.7% vs 0.5%, P=0.04). Knee extension torque increased only in the BFRRE group (P=0.04) and 1RM increased only in the control group (P=0.02); no between-group strength difference was found. Satellite cell counts did not change.",
   "limitations": "Small groups and a short intervention, with limited power for type II fibre effects. Cuff pressure was set with elastic wraps, and the strength test was front squat, a lift the powerlifters were less practised in.",
   "practicalImplications": "Short blocks of low-load blood flow-restricted squats can add quadriceps size without heavy loads, but this trial does not support expecting a maximal strength gain from them. Keep high-load training in the programme.",
   "athleteDev": "Consider short low-load blood flow-restricted squat blocks alongside heavy training when muscle size is the goal; the trial showed no strength advantage over heavy front squats.",
   "rtp": "The trial enrolled healthy elite athletes and included no injury or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status": "CORRECTED",
   "changes": [
     "paper.athleteDev: 'the trial showed no strength gain' -> no between-group strength advantage; the BFRRE group did gain knee extension torque within-group ('the BFRRE group increased their MVIT with 9.4 (0.0, 18.7) N·m (P = 0.04)')",
     "screeningLimitations: 'front squat rather than the back squat the athletes trained' -> front squat was trained in both groups but several lifters were not well familiarised with it ('several of the powerlifters were clearly not well familiarized with this variant'); added 16 vs 6 high-load sessions"
   ],
   "residualConcerns": "VL CSA group difference is P=0.04 in the abstract but P=0.03 in the results text (absolute change); the record uses the abstract value. The BFRRE load was about 24% and 31% of 1RM in weeks 1 and 3.",
   "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

23	   "abstract": "Tested whether a cloud-based ultrasound pixel-intensity score tracks vastus lateralis glycogen. Study 1 measured 14 academy rugby league players before and after a match; Study 2 measured 16 recreational men after high or low carbohydrate intake following glycogen depletion. Ultrasound scores did not track glycogen in either study.",
24	   "tldr": "The ultrasound glycogen score did not change when glycogen fell after a rugby match and did not differ between high and low glycogen states. Practitioners should not use it to judge glycogen status; biopsy remains the reference.",
25	   "methods": "Study 1: 14 academy rugby league players had vastus lateralis biopsies and ultrasound scans before and within 40 minutes after an 80-minute match. Study 2: 16 recreational men completed a randomised crossover of glycogen depletion followed by 36 hours of high or low carbohydrate intake, with biopsy and scan on day 3. Scores were compared with paired t-tests and correlated with biopsy glycogen.",
26	   "findings": "After the match, glycogen fell from 443 to 271 mmol/kg dw while the ultrasound score did not change (P=0.4); the two changes were not correlated. In Study 2, glycogen was 531 vs 252 mmol/kg dw between the high and low trials, with ultrasound scores of 56 vs 54 (P=0.9). The depletion exercise did lower ultrasound scores (P<0.001), which the authors did not link to glycogen.",
27	   "limitations": "Small samples. Study 2 had no biopsy before and after the depletion exercise, and hydration and muscle water were not controlled in Study 1. The study was partly funded by the company that sells the software.",

101	
102	Purpose: To examine the validity of ultrasound (via cloud based software that measures
103	
104	pixilation intensity according to a scale of 0-100) to non-invasively assess muscle glycogen in
105	
106	human skeletal muscle.
107	
108	Methods: In Study 1, 14 professional male rugby league players competed in an 80-minute
109	
110	competitive rugby league game. In Study 2 (in a randomized repeated measures design), 16
111	
112	
113	                                                                            D
114	recreationally active males completed an exhaustive cycling protocol to deplete muscle glycogen
115	
116	followed by 36 hours of HIGH or LOW carbohydrate intake (8 v 3 g.kg-1 body mass). In both
117	
118	
119	
120	                                                    TE
121	studies, muscle biopsies and ultrasound scans were obtained from the vastus lateralis (at 50% of
122	
123	the muscle length) before and after match play in Study 1 and at 36 h after glycogen depletion in
124	
125	Study 2. Results: Despite match play reducing (P< 0.01) muscle glycogen concentration (Pre-
126	
127	
128	
129	                            EP
130	game: 443  65; Post-game: 271  94 mmol.kg-1 dw, respectively) in Study 1, there were no
131	
132	significant changes (P=0.4) in ultrasound scores (Pre-game: 47  6, Post-game: 49  7). In
133	
134	Study 2, muscle glycogen concentration was significantly different (P < 0.01) between HIGH
135	
136	(531 ± 129 mmol.kg-1 dw) and LOW (252 ± 64 mmol.kg-1 dw) yet there was no difference (P =
137	
138	               C
139	0.9) in corresponding ultrasound scores (HIGH: 56 ± 7, LOW: 54 ± 6). In both studies, no
140	
141	
142	
143	
144	A
145	significant correlations (P>0.05) were present between changes in muscle glycogen
146	
147	
148	
149	
150	 C
151	concentration and changes in ultrasound scores. Conclusion: Data demonstrate that ultrasound
152	
153	(as based on measures of pixilation intensity) is not valid to measure muscle glycogen status
154	
155	within the physiological range (i.e. 200-500 mmol.kg-1 dw) that is applicable to exercise-induced
156	
157	muscle glycogen utilization and post-exercise muscle glycogen re-synthesis.
158	
159	
160

169	 Introduction
170	
171	It is well established that high carbohydrate (CHO) availability improves both endurance and
172	
173	high-intensity intermittent exercise performance (1). As such, the practice of CHO loading to
174	
175	super-compensate muscle glycogen stores in the day(s) immediately prior to competition remains
176	
177	the cornerstone of sport nutrition practices (2). The practice of ensuring high CHO availability
178	
179	before and during exercise emerged from the seminal studies of Bergstrom and colleagues (3-6)
180	
181	
182	                                                                            D
183	demonstrating that high muscle glycogen availability (as achieved via consumption of a high
184	
185	CHO diet) improved exercise capacity. The emergence of the muscle biopsy technique therefore
186	
187	
188	
189	                                                    TE
190	provided the platform for the following decades of research examining the regulation of
191	
192	glycogen storage and metabolism during exercise. Nonetheless, the technique of removing
193	
194	muscle tissue has associated risks due to potentially endangering neurovascular structures, thus
195	
196	
197	
198	                            EP
199	limiting its use to muscles with low vascularity such as the vastus lateralis. Complications such
200	
201	as local skin infections, arterial bleed, ecchymosis or hematoma, prolonged pain (i.e. > three
202	
203	days) and a small area of local numbness distal to the biopsy site have also been reported (7).
204	
205	Whilst the use of the microbiopsy technique is considered less invasive and painful than
206	
207	               C
208	traditional Bergstrom needles (8) the invasive nature of muscle biopsy sampling may still induce
209	
210	
211	
212	
213	A
214	complications that limit its application to elite athletic populations.
215	
216	
217	
218	
219	 C
220	The recent emergence of an ultrasound (US) technique to non-invasively assess muscle glycogen
221	
222	(9, 10) therefore holds much promise for those practitioners working at the coalface of elite
223	
224	sport. This technique is now available through commercially available cloud based software (9,
225	
226	10) and is based on the premise that glycogen storage can be assessed through its association
227	
228	with water. In this way, glycogen depletion within the muscle (and hence loss of intracellular
229	
230	water) can manifest as changes in pixilation intensity upon US imaging. In the initial study in
231	
232	                                                         3
233	
234	
235	
236	Copyright © 2019 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
237	 this area, Hill and Milan (9) observed significant correlations between changes in pixel intensity
238	
239	scores (a score ranging from 0-100) of rectus femoris ultrasound scans and changes in muscle
240	
241	glycogen concentration (as directly assessed from biopsies obtained from the rectus femoris)
242	
243	before and after 90-minutes of laboratory based steady-state cycling exercise performed at an
244	
245	intensity below lactate threshold.            Despite similar correlations and associations between
246	
247	glycogen utilisation within the vastus lateralis muscle during cycling (a laboratory-based 75-km
248	
249	
250	                                                                            D
251	time trial equating to 2-3 hours of exercise) and the ultrasound scoring system (10), there have
252	
253	been no further assessments of validity of this scoring system in either laboratory or field-based
254	
255	
256	
257	                                                    TE
258	settings. Indeed, it is important to assess the validity of such software to assess glycogen
259	
260	utilization in both laboratory-based and field-based high-intensity activity, given the potential
261	
262	differences in mechanical loads and fluid shifts that are induced by the contrasting contractile
263	
264	
265	
266	                            EP
267	stimuli. In an attempt to eliminate the potential confounding effects of acute changes in fluid
268	
269	shifts associated with differing exercise stimuli, an alternative approach to evaluate the validity
270	
271	of ultrasound is to also assess its ability to detect changes in muscle glycogen re-synthesis across
272	
273	a time-scale in which acute changes in fluid shifts have been restored to pre-exercise values. If
274

276	this approach proves valid, then the ultrasound-based technique is potentially assessing “true”

282	fluctuations in muscle glycogen as opposed to artefacts associated with acute changes in
283

288	intracellular and extracellular fluid changes.

291

293

295

453

457	
458	same limb and from separate location points (approximately ~1-2 cm proximal) and the
459

461	
462	                                                    TE
463	ultrasound scan was always performed prior to the biopsy.                          All muscle samples were
464	
465	immediately snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80OC for later analysis. Muscle
466	
467	glycogen concentration was determined through acid hydrolysis. Approximately 3-5 mg of
468	
469

483	
484

                  Ultrasound Does Not Detect Acute Changes in Glycogen

                                          in Vastus Lateralis of Man



        Harry E Routledge1, Warren J Bradley1, Sam O Shepherd1, Matthew Cocks1, Robert M

                               Erskine1,2, Graeme L Close1 and James P Morton1



1
                                                                            D
    Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences, Liverpool John Moores University,

Liverpool, United Kingdom



2
                                                          TE

Address for correspondence:
Prof James Morton

Tel: +44 151 904 6233

This study was funded in part by MuscleSound, USA. The authors declare no conflicts of
